summary: A 4-week plan to prepare for the GRE while maintaining balance with your part-time job and wellness goals.
reasoning: Based on your background as a UCLA junior studying Economics with strong quantitative skills but limited verbal confidence, this plan prioritizes verbal practice in morning sessions when focus is highest, while scheduling quantitative review during your natural peak hours after lunch.

items.title: GRE Verbal Practice - Reading Comprehension
items.purpose: Building reading comprehension skills requires fresh mental energy, making early morning ideal for this challenging section.
items.explanation: Start with one passage from the ETS Official Guide. Read actively, underlining key arguments and transitions. Answer all questions, then review explanations for both correct and incorrect choices. This deliberate practice builds pattern recognition that transfers to test day performance.

items.title: GRE Quantitative Review - Data Interpretation
items.purpose: Leveraging your strong quantitative background to refine speed and accuracy on data interpretation questions.
items.explanation: Work through 10 data interpretation questions focusing on efficiency. Your economics background gives you an advantage here. Time yourself and aim to complete each question set in under 2 minutes. Review any questions where you second-guessed yourself.

items.title: Review 20 GRE vocabulary words
items.purpose: Vocabulary building requires consistent, spaced repetition rather than marathon sessions.
items.explanation: Use flashcards or a vocabulary app to review 20 words. Focus on understanding word roots and usage in context rather than memorizing definitions. Try to use 3 new words in conversation or writing today. This approach builds lasting retention.

items.title: Complete one practice essay prompt
items.purpose: Writing fluency develops through regular practice with the specific essay formats the GRE requires.
items.explanation: Choose one Issue or Argument prompt from the ETS pool. Set a timer for 30 minutes and write a complete essay. Spend the remaining 15 minutes reviewing your structure and identifying areas where your argument could be stronger. Focus on clear thesis statements and logical paragraph flow.

items.title: Morning walk - mental clarity break
items.purpose: Physical movement before study sessions improves focus and retention.
items.explanation: A 30-minute walk before your first study session primes your brain for learning. Leave your phone at home or on airplane mode. Use this time to mentally review what you learned yesterday or preview what you will study today. This simple habit significantly improves study session quality.

items.title: Form a GRE study group
items.purpose: Peer accountability and discussion deepen understanding and maintain motivation.
items.explanation: Consider reaching out to 2-3 classmates also preparing for the GRE. Meeting once a week to discuss challenging problems or review each other's practice essays creates accountability and exposes you to different problem-solving approaches. This social element can make the preparation process more sustainable.

items.title: Full-length practice test
items.purpose: Simulating real test conditions builds stamina and identifies weak areas before the actual exam.
items.explanation: Take a complete practice test under realistic conditions. Find a quiet space, disable all notifications, and take only the breaks allowed on the real test. After completing, do not immediately check your score. Instead, note which sections felt most challenging and which questions caused you to hesitate. Review the test the following day with fresh eyes.

items.title: Research GRE score requirements for target programs
items.purpose: Knowing your target score provides clear direction and appropriate intensity for your preparation.
items.explanation: Look up the average GRE scores for admitted students at your top 5 graduate programs. Note both the median scores and the ranges. This information helps calibrate your study intensity and identify whether you need to focus more on verbal or quantitative improvement to reach your goals.
